title: A divisibility argument and its converse
stem: For an integer $n$, define $D=n^3-n$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Factorize $D$ and prove that it is divisible by 6 for every integer $n$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: A student claims: “If an integer is divisible by 6, it must equal $n^3-n$ for some integer $n$.” Disprove the claim using the integer 12.

steps.text: Of three consecutive integers, at least one is even.
Exactly one of the three is divisible by 3; together these factors give divisibility by 6.
For positive integers $n$, the successive difference is $3n(n+1)>0$; no positive integer gives a value between 6 and 24.
$n=0,1$ give zero and negative $n$ give non-positive values, so 12 is a counterexample.

answerSummary: $n^3-n$ is always a multiple of 6; the converse is false, with counterexample 12.

title: Adding sound intensities on a logarithmic scale
stem: Sound level is modelled by $L=10\log_{10}(I/I_0)$ dB. Two independent sources have levels $60$ dB and $70$ dB at a microphone. Their intensities add; $I_0$ is the same reference intensity for both.

title: When an exponential equation has one real solution
stem: The equation $4^x-k2^x+4=0$ contains a real parameter $k$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use $u=2^x$ to state a quadratic equation and the restriction on $u$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find every value of $k$ for which the original equation has exactly one real solution, and find that solution.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: For $k>4$, explain why there are exactly two distinct real solutions.

steps.text: $k=-4$ has repeated root $u=-2$, which is inadmissible; $k=4$ has repeated root $u=2$.
The discriminant is positive; the two roots have positive product 4 and positive sum $k$, so both are positive.
Each distinct positive root gives exactly one real value of $x=\log_2u$.

answerSummary: Exactly one real solution only at $k=4$, where $x=1$; two for $k>4$.

title: Perimeters and areas in nested squares
stem: A sequence of concentric squares begins with side length $8$ cm. Each following square has side length $\frac34$ of the preceding one. “Total area” below means the sum of individual square areas, counting overlaps repeatedly.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the sum of the perimeters of all the squares.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the sum of their areas.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why using the perimeter ratio in the area calculation would be wrong.

steps.text: Perimeters form a geometric series with first term 32 and ratio $3/4$.
Areas have first term 64 and ratio $(3/4)^2=9/16$.
Area scales with the square of side length, so its ratio is $9/16$, not $3/4$.
